inline.s: [Minister-officials (zǎi guān)] Originally officials subordinate to the Grand Steward in the Zhou dynasty; later a general term for government officials. [Grand Steward (zhǒng zǎi)] An office of the Zhou dynasty, first among the six ministers, also called the Grand Administrator. [Sharp repartee (jī fēng)] A Chan term. It refers to speech in question and answer that is swift and piercing, leaves no trace, and carries profound meaning. The original sense of jī fēng is the trigger mechanism and arrow-point of a crossbow; Chan uses it as a metaphor for agile and profound thought and speech. Chan practitioners often used such repartee to test the depth of another’s awakening in dialogue.

blocks.text: 36. Illness of the Body, Illness of Chan

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions for the Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng (zhuān))

[The upward path is the monk’s own proper concern. When the ancients set out and wandered beyond the regions, it was only to make this matter clear. In recent times people no longer know at all what leaving home is for — how could one expect them to match the ancients?]

The upward path is the monk’s own proper concern. When the ancients went on pilgrimage, roaming the whole world, it was only to make this matter clear. In recent times monks no longer know what leaving home is for — how could one expect them to reach the realm of the ancients?

[The Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng first studied under Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai, hearing and learning the scriptures and treatises. After a long time he cast all of it aside, took up a single thought, and earnestly investigated his own proper concern. He journeyed ten thousand li southward in search of instruction, passed through Caoxi, and called upon the Elder to ask for guidance. The Elder said: In this matter, if one does not put down body and mind and grind out the investigation with bitter effort to the place where the waters run dry and the mountains end, there will in the end be no landing place. Even when one reaches the place where waters run dry and mountains end, the ancients called it ‘still, sunken, dead water,’ and again ‘the burrow of the mysterious and wondrous.’ If one does not turn the head and shift the brain, then what stands before one is like an iron wall and a silver mountain: it is only the time of gaining power, not the place of use. The ancients’ use of mind was not to die all the way to the bottom; one must come alive within death — the key lies in turning the mechanism and shifting the position. Therefore it is said: ‘The one who does not move at the top of a hundred-foot pole
(having already reached the point where not one thought arises)
, though he may enter, has not attained the real; let him step forward once more from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the great thousand-world will appear in his body
(personally realizing the original nature)

. ’ When a student reaches this, he has no choice but to turn around and walk another road; only so will he not be obstructed by it. The Chan monk assented, bowed, and took his leave, and thereupon went to dwell among the thatch
(that is, cutting grass to build a hut)
on Mount Nanyue.]
Zhuan (
zhuān

)yu Heng, the Chan monk, first relied on Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai, hearing and studying the scriptures and treatises. After studying in this way for a long while, he resolved to lay it all down, take up a single thought, and earnestly investigate the matter of seeing his own nature. He traveled a great distance southward seeking the Way, passed through Caoxi, and called on the Elder to request instruction. The Elder said: In this matter (the upward path), if one does not put down body and mind and grind the investigation with bitter effort to the place where the waters run dry and the mountains end, there will in the end be no landing place. Even having reached the place where waters run dry and mountains end, it is only what the ancients called ‘still, sunken, dead water,’ and again named ‘the burrow of the mysterious and wondrous.’ If one does not turn the head and shift the brain, then what stands before one is like an iron wall and a silver mountain: it is only the time of gaining power, not the place of use. The ancients’ use of mind was not to die all the way to the bottom; one must come alive within death — the key lies in turning the mechanism and shifting the position. Therefore it is said: ‘The one who does not move at the top of a hundred-foot pole, though he may enter, has not attained the ultimate; let him step forward once more from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the great thousand-world will appear in his body.’ When a student reaches this, he should simply turn around and walk another road; only so will he not be obstructed by it. The Chan monk respectfully assented, bowed, and took his leave, going to Mount Nanyue to cut the wild grass and build a thatched hut for cultivation.

[The one who does not move] ‘Not moving’ means that thoughts do not move (no thought arises) — that is, not a single thought arises. ‘The one who does not move’ is a person in whom not a single thought arises.

[Before long the Elder too came leaning on his staff. On inquiring after the Chan monk, he learned that the monk had been troubled by the demon of illness and had already gone to Baoqing for medical treatment. Hearing this, the Elder sighed: ‘The Chan gate is in decline; students who truly take birth and death to heart are the hardest to find. And now this man has this illness — surely the dragons and devas have grown weary of this Dharma gate!’ In the spring of the bingchen year, on the first day of the third month, at midnight amid wind and rain, the Chan monk suddenly arrived, braving the rain and slogging through the mud. When the Elder saw him he was overjoyed and said: How could a sick man do this? Looking at his brow and countenance, brimming with clear, brisk spirit, he knew the illness was eight or nine parts cured.]

Before long the Elder (myself) also came leaning on a staff to Mount Nanyue. Asking after the Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng, he learned that the monk had been troubled by the demon of illness and had gone to Baoqing for medical treatment. The Elder sighed on hearing it: ‘The Chan gate is in decline; students who truly take birth and death to heart are the hardest to find. Now this man suffers this illness — is it not that the dragons and devas disdain this Dharma gate and withhold their protection?’ In the spring of the bingchen year, on the first day of the third month, in the middle of the night amid a raging storm, the Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng suddenly arrived, braving the rain and slogging through mud. The Elder met him and said with great joy: How is this a sick man? Looking at his brow and countenance, brimming with clear, brisk spirit, he therefore knew that his illness was already eight or nine parts cured.

[He therefore again offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Elder specially told him: Your demon of illness is your great good friend, a contributing condition for the Way — do you understand? Indeed, the illness of sentient beings lies in having a self. Because they cling to a self, all afflictions and manifold illnesses arise from it. When illness arises, suffering must follow. From ancient times to the present, there is no one who is not sick with this. Only the person who understands illness as illness is not ill. Moreover, the four great elements are a false union: whatever gathers must scatter — even if one is not ill, how is one ever not ill? If one understands the one who is not ill within illness, then illness cannot make one ill. You know today’s illness, but you do not know the illness of many lives, kalpa after kalpa, that has been ailing up to today. If you do not understand today’s illness, then from now on you will never know where illness ends.]

He therefore again offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Elder specially told him: Your demon of illness is your great good friend, a contributing condition for the Way — do you know this? The illness of sentient beings lies in having a self. Because of clinging to a self, all afflictions and manifold illnesses arise. When illness arises, suffering must follow. From ancient times to now, there is no one who is not ill from this. Only one who knows why illness is illness will not be made ill by illness. Moreover, the four great elements are a false union; whatever gathers must scatter — even if one is not ill, how is one ever not ill? If one understands that the root of illness is the self, and does not cling to the self, then sickness cannot make one sick. You know today’s illness, but you do not know the illness of many lives, kalpa upon kalpa of the illness of ‘having a self,’ up to today. If you do not understand today’s illness of ‘having a self,’ then from now on you will never know how to put an end to illness.
[Illness as illness] The first ‘illness’ is a verb; the second ‘illness’ is its object.

[You know the illness of birth and death, but you do not know the illness of wanting to escape birth and death — which is far greater than the illness of birth and death itself. Why is this? The ancients held that when Chan practice does not go beyond the realm of the aggregates and falls into the trap of consciousness and emotion, then even a wonderful awakening becomes a view of self. When one clings to the four elements as the self, the illness can still be cured; but now, having left the four elements behind, one again clings to there being a self — this illness leaves even the King of Physicians helpless, the hardest of all to treat. All the Buddhas and patriarchs came into the world expressly to cure this one terminal disease; though they spent untold effort of mind, how many are there who are willing to take the medicine and be cured?]

You know only the illness of birth and death, but you do not know that the practice for escaping birth and death is itself also diseased — and far more serious and harder to cure. Why? The ancients held that if Chan practice does not go beyond the realm of the aggregates and falls into the trap of consciousness and emotion, then even a wonderful awakening only builds up a view of self. Because one clings to the four elements as the self, the illness can still be treated; but now, having left the four elements behind, one again clings to there being a self — this illness leaves even the King of Physicians with no recourse, the hardest of all to treat. All the Buddhas and patriarchs came into the world expressly to cure this one terminal disease. Though they spent immeasurable effort of mind, how many are there who are willing to take the medicine and be cured?

[The realm of the aggregates (yīn jiè)] The five aggregates and the eighteen elements. The five aggregates are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The eighteen elements are the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, together with the six dusts of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects, and the six consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [A disease beyond cure (gāo huāng zhī bìng)] A terminal illness. [To be cured (
chài
To recover from illness.

[The Chan monk’s bodily illness is cured; on no account may he be invaded by the illness of Chan. Yunmen said that the dharma-body has two kinds of illness. His words ‘penetrating the dharma-body’ — if attachment to dharmas is not forgotten and one’s own views still remain, that too is illness — are an emphatic statement of the illness of clinging and grasping. Let the Chan monk spit out together all the mysterious words and wondrous sayings he previously accumulated, along with the merit he guarded and clung to in Chan practice, until not a trace of evil perception or evil habit remains; then he will certainly not let them grow into a root of illness, and will straightaway leave the Buddhas and patriarchs no place to stand. Have you not seen Sudhana, who journeyed south through a hundred cities and studied under fifty-three great good friends, each granting him one Dharma gate, and in the end came away only with something equal to the Dharma realm and equal to empty space — was there ever any real dharma tied to him? And have you not seen Vairocana, whose dharma-body is no body, but who takes the wonderful practice of Samantabhadra as his body? Samantabhadra has no practice; he takes the practice of sentient beings as his practice. Therefore it is said: That on which bodhi depends is suffering sentient beings; if there were no sentient beings, there would be no bodhi. This is the true model of the Buddhas and patriarchs of former times coming into the world.]

Chan monk (you), your bodily illness is cured; by no means may you be invaded by the illness of Chan. Yunmen (Chan Master Wenyan) said the dharma-body has two kinds of illness: in penetrating the dharma-body, if attachment to dharmas is not forgotten and one’s own views still remain, that too is illness — this is his utmost statement on the illness of clinging and grasping. You must cast away (spit out) all the mysterious words and wondrous sayings you previously accumulated, along with the fruits of merit (gōng xūn) you guarded and clung to in Chan practice, until not a trace of evil perception or evil habit remains; then you will certainly not let them grow into a root of illness, and will straightaway leave the Buddhas and patriarchs no place to stand. Have you not seen Sudhana, who journeyed south through a hundred cities and studied under fifty-three great good friends, each granting him one Dharma gate, and in the end came away only with something equal to the Dharma realm and equal to empty space — was there ever any real dharma tied to him? And have you not seen Vairocana Buddha, whose dharma-body is no body, but who takes the wonderful practice of Samantabhadra as his body? Samantabhadra has no practice; he takes the practice of sentient beings as his practice. Therefore it is said: That on which bodhi depends is suffering sentient beings; if there were no sentient beings, there would be no bodhi. This is the true model of the Buddhas and patriarchs of former times coming into the world.

[The two kinds of illness of the dharma-body] Yunmen said: “The dharma-body likewise has two kinds of illness: attaining the dharma-body, yet not forgetting attachment to dharmas and still holding one’s own views, is falling beside the dharma-body — that is one; even if one penetrates it thoroughly, one must not let it go. Examining it carefully, whatever breath or trace remains is also illness.” [Merit (gōng xūn)] The fruits of practice. [Vairocana] Vairocana is the dharmakāya Buddha, Locana the saṃbhogakāya Buddha, and Śākyamuni the nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Among the “ten Buddha names” there is: “Vairocana Buddha, pure dharmakāya; Locana Buddha, perfect saṃbhogakāya; Śākyamuni Buddha, transformation body in hundreds of thousands of millions.” [The ten Buddha names] The names of the Buddhas chanted at the two meals of porridge and rice each day, also called “the ten recitations at mealtime.” “Ten Buddhas” is an approximate number; in practice more than ten are chanted. [The three bodies] Dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya. The dharmakāya is also called the body of self-nature, or the body of dharma-nature: it is the permanent, indestructible true nature that everyone originally possesses; it is only that we sentient beings are deluded and do not manifest it, while the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The saṃbhogakāya is formed from the Buddha’s wisdom and merit, and is divided into the saṃbhogakāya for his own enjoyment and the saṃbhogakāya for others’ enjoyment: the former is the body in which the Buddha himself enjoys the bliss of inner realization, the latter the body manifested to teach the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The nirmāṇakāya is also called the body of response and transformation, or the body of transformation: the Buddha-body manifested in response to the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

[The Elder therefore said to the Chan monk: The diseased body of the four elements can only be cured by the demon of illness; the illness of Chan that pierces the heart can only be cured by sentient beings. From today on, simply make the body equal to the great earth, and the demon of illness will hide its traces. Make the mind equal to sentient beings, and the view of self will not stand. When the view of self does not stand, the illness of Chan dissolves of itself. Because the mind does not mind itself, it is originally unborn. Being unborn, not a single dharma is established. If not a single dharma is established, what dharma is there to become an obstruction of views? The ancients said: To renounce emotion is easy; to renounce dharmas is hard. The Chan monk renounces the body, which is to renounce emotion; renounces views, which is to renounce dharmas. With emotion and dharmas both forgotten, is he not a person of great, unobstructed liberation? Alas, I am old, and to meet again will be hard. Strive on, Chan monk.]

The Elder therefore said to the Chan monk: As for the illness of this diseased body of the four elements, apart from the demon of illness there is no curing it; as for the illness of Chan that pierces the heart, apart from sentient beings there is no curing it. From today on, simply make the body equal to the great earth, and the demon of illness will hide its traces. Make the mind equal to sentient beings, and the view of self will not stand. When the view of self does not stand, the illness of Chan dissolves of itself. Because the mind arises dependent on form and cannot exist independently, it is originally unborn. Being unborn, not a single dharma is established. If not a single dharma is established, what dharma is there to become an obstruction of views? The ancients said: To renounce emotion is easy; to renounce dharmas is hard. The Chan monk renounces the body, which is to renounce emotion; renounces views, which is to renounce dharmas. With emotion and dharmas both forgotten, is he not a person of great, unobstructed liberation? Alas, I am old, and to meet again will be hard. Strive on, Chan monk.

[The diseased body of the four elements can only be cured by the demon of illness] As for the illness of this diseased body of the four elements, apart from the demon of illness there is no curing it. For the demon of illness makes one realize that the body of form is illusory and is not oneself, while the root of the diseased body of the four elements is the deluded clinging to the body of form as “I” (as a self). Just as Master Hanshan taught earlier: “Your demon of illness is your great good friend, a contributing condition for the Way — do you know this? Indeed, the illness of sentient beings lies in having a self. Because they cling to a self, all afflictions and manifold illnesses arise from it.” [Because the mind does not mind itself, it is originally unborn] The mind arises dependent on form and cannot exist independently, and so is originally unborn. Mazu said: “Whatever form is seen is the seeing of mind; the mind does not mind itself — it exists because of form.” (Wudeng Huiyuan)
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Inscription on Clarifying the Mind, for Ding Youwu)
The key to clarifying the mind is the absence of the mark of self.
[The true nature, deep and serene, like water stilled and clear; struck by hate and love, waves of affliction appear.]
The original nature is serene and profound, like stilled, limpid water; when hate and love stir it, waves of affliction rise.
[Stirred without cease, the self-nature turns unclear; affliction and ignorance but deepen, unaware.]

Stirred without cease, the self-nature therefore grows turbid (the self-nature falls into a state of dullness); and because the self-nature is turbid (dull), affliction and ignorance only increase while one remains unaware.
[Increasing while unaware] They increase while one is unaware. If one were aware, affliction and ignorance could not increase.
[Grasping the other through the I, like mud mixed into water; letting the other stir the I, like oil that feeds the fire.]

Once the mark of self is established, “this” and “that” appear: it is like mud mixed into pure water, and the self-nature grows all the more turbid. Letting love and hate for the other stir me is like adding oil to fire, making the fire of affliction and ignorance fiercer and more blazing.
[Oil] Lamp oil. [The other] Other people and outer objects.
[The other troubles my true nature; the trouble springs from ‘I.’ If ‘I’ is never born, the kalpa-fire freezes to ice.]
The other disturbs my true nature (original nature); in fact the disturbance is born of the “I” (the mark of self). If the “I” is not born, the fire of the kalpa turns to ice.
[The kalpa burning] The great conflagration that occurs at the time of the destruction kalpa, burning up to the heaven of the first dhyāna, reducing everything to ashes.
[Therefore the sage first empties the mark of self; the mark of self once empty, from where can the other obstruct?]

For this reason, the sage (the person of the highest attainment) first empties out the mark of self; if the mark of self is empty, how can the other (other people and outer objects) become an obstruction?
[The sage (zhì rén)] A person who has reached the highest realm.
[To forget the self, hold firm and patiently endure; the moment habit stirs, wake suddenly and sure.]
Doing the work of forgetting the self depends on firm and patient endurance; the moment a habitual tendency arises, one wakes with a sudden start.
[Where one wakes is awareness: a single thought turns back its light, sweeping away all traces, leaving no track in sight; and in that very instant, all is cool and bright.]

The place where one wakes is awareness itself: with a single thought of turning the light back to shine within, habitual tendencies are swept away without trace, and one is immediately cool and clear.

[Where one wakes is awareness] The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has marks is deceptive.” “No mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a life span.” “All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; they should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all.” First one should take these three as the outline and earnestly do the work of wisdom’s contemplation, seeing through and letting go. Chan Master Guifeng said: “Awaken to all marks as empty, and the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, be aware; being aware, it is at once gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies nowhere else.” (Preface to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan) The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing the illusory, one at once departs from it, without resort to means; departing from the illusory is itself awakening, with no gradual stages.”
[Cool, still, and quiet; upright, standing alone; calm and joyous in spirit — no thing can be its foe.]
Cool, still, and quiet; upright and standing alone (keeping no company with the ten thousand dharmas); tranquil and serene, gladdening the spirit — no thing can be its match.

[Things] People and circumstances other than oneself. [No thing can match it] Since one no longer stands opposed to things, one is naturally not defeated by them. This is the state that transcends the ten thousand things (keeping no company with the ten thousand dharmas).

Fei’ means spending effort and time; ‘xian’ means useless. Feixian, then, is to spend energy and time without any real result — what is commonly called doing useless work. In the Song of Wasted Idleness, Master Hanshan points out the pitfalls in practice where effort and time are squandered, and how to step out of them.

[To preach the Way is easy, to embody it hard; if stray thoughts are not cleared, all practice is marred. When worldly toil and dust still snag the breast, then sitting deep in mountains is but wasted rest.]

It is easy to preach the Way to others but hard to practice it oneself; if stray thoughts are not cleared away, everything is idle (effort wasted); if worldly toil and dust constantly snag the mind, then sitting in quiet in deep mountains is in vain.

[To embody the Way] To practice (personally carry out) the right Way. To preach the Way without personally walking it means one cannot truly realize the Way; and if one misleads students, it brings great evil consequences for both others and oneself. [Zongshi] All of it. [All is idle] All of it is useless. [In vain] To no purpose, futilely; for example: to waste effort to no purpose.

[To leave home is easy, to keep the rule is hard; with neither faith nor vow, all effort is marred. The pure precepts unkept, one labours but in vain; though one has shaved one’s head, it is but loss and pain.]

Leaving home is easy, but keeping the precepts and rules is hard; with no faith or vow at all, everything is idle; if the pure precepts are not kept, one labours in vain; though one shaves one’s head and leaves home, it is still futile.
[To practice is easy, to find a teacher hard; lacking a true teacher, all effort is marred. Clever in one’s own conceit, one toils in vain; blind and sightless practice is but loss and pain.]

Practice is easy, but meeting a teacher is hard; without meeting an illumined teacher, everything is idle; being clever in one’s own conceit is wasted effort; blind, sightless cultivation is also futile.

[To be stained is easy, to be free of stain is hard; if worldly toil is not cut off, all effort is marred. Clinging with passion and habit, one spends one’s strength in vain; the fruit of the Way unattained — it is but loss and pain.]

It is easy to be stained by dust but hard to get out of the dust; if worldly toil is not cut off, everything is idle; to cling and climb with passion and habit is wasted effort; failing to attain the fruit of the Way is also futile.

[Worldly toil (chén láo)] The mind toiling over the dusts of sense objects; another name for affliction. [Climbing with passion and habit] To climb after and fabricate things with emotional consciousness and habitual tendencies, mistaking it for practice.

[To hear is easy, to be true-hearted hard; to slight and scorn one’s teacher — all effort marred. Proud and puffed up, one spends one’s strength in vain; though wit outshine the world, it is but loss and pain.]

It is easy to hear the teachings but hard to practice them with a true heart; to slight and scorn one’s teacher is always idle; to be proud and arrogant is wasted effort; though one’s cleverness cover the world, it is also futile.
[Proud and high (gòng gāo)] To think oneself a cut above others.
[To study the Way is easy, to awaken to it hard; if no effort is made, all is idle, all is marred. To believe but not practice is strength spent in vain; mere empty talk is also loss and pain.]
Studying the Way is easy but awakening to the Way is hard; not putting in effort is always idle; being able to believe but not to practice is wasted effort; empty talk and discussion is also futile.

[To shut the gate is easy, to keep the gate is hard; if one refuses to practice, all effort is marred. Body within the gate, the mind outside — one toils in vain; a thousand years without emerging is but loss and pain.]

Secluding oneself is easy, but practicing earnestly inside the retreat is hard; refusing to practice steadily is always idle; with the body inside the gate and the mind outside, a thousand years without leaving the retreat is also futile.

[To recite the Buddha is easy, to have true faith is hard; with heart and mouth not one, all effort is marred. The mouth recites Amitābha, the mind is all astray; though the throat be shouted hoarse, it is but waste of day.]

Reciting the Buddha’s name is easy, but a faithful and true heart is hard; when heart and mouth are not one (the heart is not sincere: the mouth recites the Buddha while the mind thinks of other things) everything is idle (all wasted effort); to recite Amitābha with the mouth while the mind wanders is futile even if one shouts the throat raw.

[True and sincere] Honest, not deceitful. “A heart of faith” means a heart that is true and sincere; when heart and mouth are not one, that is falsehood. Hence the next line: “when heart and mouth are not one, all is idle.”

[To bow to the Buddha is easy, to revere is hard; when the intent is not devout, all effort is marred. The five limbs bowing empty, one toils in vain; though the skull be cracked open, it is but loss and pain.]

Bowing to the Buddha is easy, but a reverent heart is hard; when the intent is not devout, everything is idle; the five limbs (two hands, two knees, and the head) bowing hollowly (without reverence) is wasted effort; though the skull (the shell without a mind) be cracked open, it is also futile.

[To recite sutras is easy, to understand them hard; to chant with the mouth but not understand — all effort marred. To understand but not follow is strength spent in vain; though ten thousand scrolls be chanted daily, it is but loss and pain.]

Reciting sutras is easy but understanding them is hard; to recite with the mouth without understanding is always idle; to understand but not to practice is wasted effort; though one recites ten thousand scrolls a day, it is also futile.
(From The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions for Zhou Yangru)

[Turning consciousness into wisdom] To turn the ordinary person’s defiled eight consciousnesses into the Buddha’s four wisdoms: that is, to turn the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the seventh (manas) into the Wisdom of Equality, the sixth (mental consciousness) into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the first five (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness) into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done.

[Master Zhou asked for instruction on the essential purport of the Dharma-character school, and the Elder therefore brought up the Sixth Patriarch’s Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom: “The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror. The fifth and eighth, the sixth and seventh, turn at the fruit and at the cause; but only the names turn — there is no real nature. If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment, then amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi.”]

Master Zhou requested instruction on the essential purport of the Dharma-character school, so the Elder brought up the Sixth Patriarch’s Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom: “The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror. The fifth and eighth, the sixth and seventh, turn at the fruit and at the cause; but only the names turn — there is no real nature. If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment, then amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi.”

[Master Zhou] “Zi” was an ancient honorific for a person. [The Dharma-character school] One of the eight great schools of the Mahāyāna; because it exhaustively clarifies the nature and characteristics of the ten thousand dharmas, it is called the Dharma-character school. Since it relies on the Consciousness-Only treatises to clarify the principle that the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only, it is also called the Consciousness-Only school. [The eight schools] The Vinaya school, the Huayan school, the Tiantai school, the Three-Treatise school (the Dharma-nature school), the Dharma-character school (the Consciousness-Only school), the Mantra school, the Chan school, and the Pure Land school.

To make Master Hanshan’s teaching below easier to understand, the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom that the Sixth Patriarch set forth in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch are first explained as follows:

[The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror.]

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind free of illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation perceives without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror.

[The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature] The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) turns into. The ālaya stores immeasurable karmic seeds and exerts a defiling influence on feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Now, with consciousness turned into wisdom, it no longer defiles, and so it is said to be “pure in nature.” [The Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness] The Wisdom of Equality is what the seventh consciousness (manas) turns into. The chief function of manas is to think, measure, and calculate, which is the great illness that brings about birth and death. Now, with consciousness turned into wisdom, it no longer thinks, measures, and calculates, and so it is said to be “a mind without illness.” [The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort] The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation is what the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness) turns into. The chief function of the mental consciousness is to exercise discrimination when the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) meet the corresponding five dusts (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch). Now, with consciousness turned into wisdom, it merely observes and no longer discriminates, and so it is said that “seeing is without effort” (in seeing there is likewise no function of discrimination). [The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror] The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is what the first five consciousnesses turn into; once they become wisdom, they merely reflect the objects before them without discriminating, and so it is said to be “like a round mirror.”

[The fifth and eighth, the sixth and seventh, turn at the fruit and at the cause; but it is only names that turn — there is no real nature. If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment, then amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi.]

The sixth and seventh consciousnesses turn on the level of cause, while the first five and the eighth are naturally accomplished on the level of fruit (at the time of becoming Buddha). This turning (turning the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms) merely turns their names and characteristics (their state); the essence is not two (it has no real nature). If at the point where (the sixth and seventh consciousnesses) turn from consciousness into wisdom one keeps no attachment, turning decisively and resolutely (this is precisely where the work is done in daily life), then even amid the swirling red dust of the world one is like a dragon hidden in the deep pool, coiled and unmoving, forever abiding in nāga samādhi.

[The level of fruit] As opposed to “the level of cause”: the fruition attained by practicing on the level of cause. Here the fruition means the fruit of Buddhahood. [Teeming activity (fán xīng)] Arising in great number; here it means the myriad phenomena in their profusion. [Nāga samādhi] “Nāga” is translated as “dragon.” “Nāga samādhi” is “dragon samādhi” — like a dragon lurking in a deep pool, coiled and unmoving. [If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment] Turning with not the slightest stagnation, like a poisonous snake biting one’s finger: cut it off at once. [Amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi] Though placed amid the swirling red dust of the world with its myriad phenomena (teeming activity), one forever abides in dragon samādhi.
The main text of this chapter now continues:

[These eight lines lay bare the very heart and marrow of the Buddhas and patriarchs and reveal the root source of nature and characteristics. Yet those who count another’s treasures and tally grains of sand, greedy for much and unable to chew what they bite off, generally regard this as idle furniture and have never once looked at it with a true eye — how greatly to be pitied!]

These eight lines of the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom lay bare the very heart and marrow of the Buddhas and patriarchs and reveal the root source of nature and characteristics. Yet those who circle endlessly among names and characteristics without true practice (those who count treasures and tally sand), greedy for much and unable to chew what they bite off (never tasting the true flavor within), all regard this as idle furniture and have never once looked at it closely with a true eye — truly a great pity.

[Counting treasures] Counting another’s treasures; it refers to those who do not truly practice according to the teachings but merely show off with their lips. [Tallying sand] To enter the sea and, instead of gathering treasures, go about counting grains of sand; it refers to those who sink into names and characteristics instead of awakening to the Way through practice.

[People all say the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate and unlearned in the teachings — how could he speak of this? They little know that the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and patriarchs is fully contained, with nothing left over, in just eight words: “The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” Because they are mind only, the three realms are quiescent, utterly without a thing; because they are consciousness only, the ten thousand dharmas stand in profusion. For the ten thousand dharmas are merely manifested from consciousness only, and when one seeks them in one’s own mind, the self-nature is utterly unattainable. That is why the Buddhas and patriarchs, in teaching people, said only that outside the mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable — which is precisely what Huangmei brought forth at midnight as “originally there is not a single thing.” In this one phrase, all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times and all the patriarchs of successive generations are contained; it cannot be broken apart, and so the robe and bowl were entrusted to him. Even the two branches and five houses all derive from this one phrase — where was there ever a division into the nature school and the characteristics school?]

They imagine that since the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate and unlearned in the scriptures, how could he reveal the root source of nature and characteristics? They little know that the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and patriarchs is fully contained, with nothing left over, in just eight words: “The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” Because they are mind only, the three realms are quiescent, utterly without a thing; because they are consciousness only, the ten thousand dharmas stand in ordered profusion. Since the ten thousand dharmas are all manifested from consciousness, when one seeks them in one’s own mind, the essence of the ten thousand dharmas (the self-nature) is utterly unattainable. Therefore what the Buddha and the patriarchs taught people was nothing more than that outside the mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable — which is precisely Huineng’s “originally there is not a single thing.” In this one phrase, all that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times and the patriarchs of successive generations said is contained; this is an irrefutable truth, and therefore the Fifth Patriarch transmitted the robe and bowl to him. Even the two branches and five houses all evolved from this one phrase — when was there ever a division between the nature school and the characteristics school?
[For the ten thousand dharmas are merely manifested from consciousness only] The Dream-Wandering Collection
Master Hanshan’s own preface and chronological record says:
“Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Depending on consciousness, one is defiled; depending on wisdom, one is pure. Defilement has birth and death; purity has no Buddhas.”

[Huangmei at midnight brought forth “originally there is not a single thing”] When Huineng spoke this essential purport of the Buddhadharma, “originally there is not a single thing,” the Fifth Patriarch thereupon transmitted the patriarch’s seat to him at midnight. Hence the saying: on Mount Huangmei at midnight a patriarch of “originally there is not a single thing” suddenly popped up. [Huangmei] Mount Huangmei, where the East Chan Monastery of Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan, was located. [The two branches] Under the Fifth Patriarch there were two branches: the Northern school of Shenxiu and the Southern school of Huineng. The watershed between these two branches is whether or not one has awakened to the truth “originally there is not a single thing.” [The five houses] Under the Sixth Patriarch there were five houses (also called the five families): the Weiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan houses. [The nature school and the characteristics school] That is, the Dharma-nature school and the Dharma-character school. 1. The Dharma-nature school (the Three-Treatise school among the eight schools), abbreviated as the nature school: it breaks through the marks of the ten thousand dharmas and reveals their true nature of emptiness and quiescence. 2. The Dharma-character school (the Consciousness-Only school), abbreviated as the characteristics school: it traces the arising of the ten thousand dharmas back to the ālaya-vijñāna, takes the ālaya-vijñāna as the root of all defiled and pure cause and effect, and extensively distinguishes the names and meanings of the dharmas it produces; hence it is called the Dharma-character school.

[Then, looking into the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom, I annotated and broke them open a little. If one takes it as “the three realms are mind only,” then there is no place to set one’s mouth. Because one is deluded about this mind and it transforms into consciousness, it loses the name of true suchness and is merely called ālaya-vijñāna, also called the storehouse consciousness; this consciousness is what the whole of true suchness transforms into. It is precisely what is meant by “born of the union of the born-and-destroyed with the unborn-and-undestroyed” — the root of the real and the false, of delusion and awakening, the basis of birth and death, of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra says: “The ocean of the storehouse consciousness is forever abiding; moved by the wind of objects, great waves surge through the dark abyss, with never a moment of cessation.” Since it says the storehouse consciousness is the ālaya, and yet says it is forever abiding, then it is fundamentally unmoving. What moves, then, is not the storehouse consciousness but only the wind of objects.]

Now the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom are used to elucidate the principle that “the three realms are mind only and the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” If one takes it in terms of “the three realms are mind only” (all that the three realms contain is simply one mind), then there is no place to set one’s mouth. Because one is deluded about this mind (true suchness) and it transforms into consciousness, it loses the name of true suchness and is merely called ālaya-vijñāna, also called the storehouse consciousness; this consciousness is what the whole of true suchness transforms into. This is precisely what is meant by “born of the union of the born-and-destroyed with the unborn-and-undestroyed” — the root of the real and the false, of delusion and awakening, the basis of birth and death, of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “The ocean of the storehouse consciousness is forever abiding; moved by the wind of objects, great waves surge through the dark abyss, with never a moment of cessation.” In the scripture, since it speaks of the storehouse consciousness (that is, the ālaya-vijñāna) and also says it is forever abiding, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally unmoving. Therefore what moves is not the storehouse consciousness but the wind of objects.

[The verse says, “If the object before is absent, the mind too is absent.” If so, then what grasps objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the mind of birth and death. This mind of birth and death is provisionally named the seventh consciousness; in fact it is the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness, what is called the vital impulse. Once this impulse is stilled, the objects before one are at once empty, and though the sixth consciousness is able to discriminate, it has nothing to fasten on. As for the first five consciousnesses, they have no separate substance of their own; they are merely the functioning of the storehouse consciousness in response to conditions, able only to reflect objects and unable to discriminate — hence “like a round mirror.” What discriminates the five dusts is not the five consciousnesses but the mental consciousness arising at the same moment as them; hence it is credited with the merit. If it does not give rise to discrimination, then “seeing is without effort.”]

The verse says: “If the object before is absent, the mind too is absent.” Therefore what grasps objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the mind of birth and death. This mind of birth and death is tentatively named the seventh consciousness (manas); in fact it is the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness (the storehouse consciousness), what is called the vital impulse. Once this vital impulse (the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness) is stilled, the objects before one are at once empty, and even though the sixth consciousness (the mental consciousness) is able to discriminate, it has nothing to fasten on (there is nothing for it to discriminate). As for the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness), they have no separate substance; they are merely the functioning of the storehouse consciousness in response to conditions. These first five consciousnesses can only reflect the dusts of objects, not discriminate them — hence “like a round mirror.” What discriminates the five dusts (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch) is not the first five consciousnesses but the sixth consciousness (the mental consciousness) arising at the same moment as them; hence it is said that the sixth consciousness is credited with the merit. If it (the sixth consciousness) does not give rise to discrimination, then “seeing is without effort.”

[Once this impulse is stilled] Once this vital impulse (the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness) is stilled. The passage above says, “in fact it is the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness, what is called the vital impulse.” “Impulse” (jī) is that from which the changes of things arise.

[Seen in this way, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally real, and so it is said to be pure in nature; its fault lies in a single thought giving rise to mind, and this is the illness of the mind. Where there is birth there is destruction; this very birth-and-destruction is like the flowing of water — there is no separate flow apart from the water. Yet the water’s nature of not abiding is what makes the mark of flowing appear; and where there is flowing, it is clear that it is not the water of a deep, still pool. Hence the Laṅkāvatāra speaks of two kinds of arising, abiding, and destruction: the arising, abiding, and destruction of marks, and the arising, abiding, and destruction of outflowing. These two kinds of birth and destruction both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If birth and destruction are not destroyed, then the first seven consciousnesses arise; if birth and destruction are destroyed, then only a single pure reality remains, and the nature of true suchness is restored from that point on. When it is restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom; hence it is said to be “a mind without illness.”]

Seen in this way, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally real, and so it is said to be pure in nature; its fault lies in a single thought giving rise to mind, and this is the illness of the mind. Where there is birth there is destruction; this very birth-and-destruction is like the flowing of water — there is no separate flow apart from the water. But this water has the nature of not abiding, and so the mark of flowing appears; where there is flowing, it is clear that it is not the still water of a deep pool. Hence the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra speaks of two kinds of arising, abiding, and destruction for the consciousnesses: the arising, abiding, and destruction of marks, and the arising, abiding, and destruction of outflowing. These two kinds of birth and destruction both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If birth and destruction are not destroyed, the first seven consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mental, and manas consciousness) arise; if birth and destruction are destroyed, the first seven consciousnesses cease, and only the storehouse consciousness, this single pure reality, remains, and the nature of true suchness is restored from then on. Once restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom; hence it is said to be “a mind without illness.”

[What the Sixth Patriarch set forth in his verses concerns the turning of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness turns into, the Wisdom of Equality what the seventh consciousness turns into, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation what the sixth consciousness turns into, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done what the first five consciousnesses turn into; because the false is the functioning of the storehouse consciousness, the true too is like a round mirror. Yet the sixth and seventh consciousnesses turn first on the level of cause, while the first five and the eighth, being one body, are perfected only at the level of fruit. Looked at in this way, consciousness is fundamentally unreal, and falsely has two functions; hence it is said that only the names turn — the name changes but not the substance. Moreover, this substance does not lie in Chan concentration and practice, but only in all the activities of daily life, where sage and ordinary turn it at the same time, and where the only difference lies in whether one keeps attachment or not; hence the distinction between sage and ordinary, delusion and awakening. Master Zhou, if you have set your will on this, earnestly fix your eye on where the turning happens in daily life, and try to settle it clearly.]

The verses composed by the Sixth Patriarch speak of turning the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness turns into, the Wisdom of Equality what the seventh consciousness (manas) turns into, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation what the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness) turns into, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done what the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) turn into; because the first five consciousnesses are the false functioning of the storehouse consciousness, when they are now turned into wisdom they are, together with the wisdom into which the storehouse consciousness is turned, the same round mirror. Yet the sixth and seventh consciousnesses turn first on the level of cause, while the first five and the eighth, being one body, turn into wisdom only on the level of fruit (at the time of becoming Buddha). Looked at in this way, the eight consciousnesses are fundamentally unreal, and falsely possess the two functions of birth-and-destruction and non-birth-and-destruction; hence it is said that only the name turns — the name changes but not the substance. Moreover, the transformation of this substance does not lie in Chan concentration and practice, but only in every arising of thought and movement of mind in daily life. Ordinary beings and sages (bodhisattvas above the first ground) alike turn it where thought arises and mind moves; ultimately, whether one is turning wisdom into consciousness or consciousness into wisdom depends only on whether one keeps attachment, and from this come the distinctions between ordinary and sage, deluded and awakened. Master Zhou, since you have set your will on this, earnestly fix your eye on where the turning happens in daily use, and look closely: are you turning rightly (turning consciousness into wisdom) or turning backwards (turning wisdom into consciousness)?

[Only the names turn — the name changes but not the substance] This means that the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms are two states of one substance, just as ice and water seem utterly different and so bear the names “ice” and “water,” when in fact they are only
H₂O
in two states — one substance, two states. When ice melts into water the name changes, but the substance is still
H₂O

, and so it is “only the names turn — the name changes but not the substance.” [Sage and ordinary turn it at the same time; the only difference lies in whether one keeps attachment] The sages, being awakened, keep no attachment toward greed, hatred, and delusion, and so are turning consciousness into wisdom; ordinary beings, being deluded, have not let go their attachment (keep attachment) toward greed, hatred, and delusion, and so do the opposite, turning wisdom into consciousness. [Sage] From the ordinary person’s practice to the attainment of Buddhahood there are fifty-two stages in all: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal awakening, and wondrous awakening. Among them, the bodhisattvas of the ten dwellings, ten practices, and ten dedications have only cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, and still have the delusions of dust-and-sand and of ignorance; they are called “worthy.” Bodhisattvas from the first ground upward have stilled the false and merged with the real, meeting the true; they are called “sages.”
(From The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions for the Chan monk Dongwen Fasheng)

[Dongwen Fasheng was long since endowed with a superior root. Having just left worldly ties, he met the Water-Flood Crane. After a while he saw that this was not right, and so abandoned him. He entered Mount Tianmu and, with the chief seat Xingrong and others, built a hut and dwelt there, polishing among themselves the matter beneath their own feet, enduring firmly for several years. He then studied under Chan Master Daguan, staying close to him for some time. Because his mind of loathing clamor and seeking stillness was not yet forgotten, he took his leave and hid himself at Luoxi. Now he has come specially to call on the Elder in this miasmal region, seeking the Dharma gate of the mind-ground.]

The Chan monk Dongwen Fasheng was long since endowed with a superior root. When he first left home he took Lanfeng as his teacher. Before long he discovered that what this man taught was not the right Dharma, and so he abandoned him and left. He entered Mount Tianmu and, with the chief seat Xingrong and others, built a hut and dwelt there, polishing among themselves the matter beneath their own feet (the great matter of birth and death), enduring firmly for several years. He also studied under Master Zibai, staying close to him for some time. Because his mind of loathing clamor and seeking stillness was not yet forgotten, he took his leave and hid himself at Luoxi. Now he has come specially to call on the Elder in this miasmal region, seeking the Dharma gate of the mind-ground.

[The Elder, following the Brahmā Net Sutra, conferred on him the Vajra Precious Precepts. Fasheng threw himself down in full prostration like Mount Tai collapsing — such was his diligence for the Dharma. Because the Elder had long drunk the miasmal mists and the four elements were impaired, he closed the gate and withdrew his traces, cultivating stillness to rest. Fasheng too bowed and returned to the mountain, having requested the conferral of the precepts.]

The Elder, following the Brahmā Net Sutra, conferred on him the Vajra Precious Precepts. Fasheng prostrated himself with the five limbs to the ground like Mount Tai collapsing — such was his diligence for the Dharma. Because the Elder had long drunk the miasmal mists and the four elements were out of harmony and impaired (he was ill), he closed the gate and withdrew his traces, cultivating stillness to rest and recover. Fasheng likewise took his leave and returned to the mountain, and so requested the conferral of the precepts.

[Water-Flood Crane] This refers to Iron-Beak Lanfeng. The original note at the end of this text says: “Dongwen first took Iron-Beak Lanfeng as his teacher. The ‘Water-Flood Crane’ mentioned here refers to Lanfeng.” [Vajra Precious Precepts] That is, the Mahāyāna bodhisattva precepts set forth in the Brahmā Net Sutra. Also called the single-mind vajra precepts. They are the intrinsically possessed, uncreated precepts of the one mind: once obtained, never lost, possessing incomparable great function. The Brahmā Net Sutra says: “The Vajra Precious Precepts are the source of all Buddhas, the source of all bodhisattvas.” [Precepts] That which guards the body and mind against transgression.

[He therefore taught him, saying: The Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings — scaled, shelled, and feathered — down to those in the hells and the three evil paths, and even those utterly dispersed and sunk in emptiness: none of them are not joined eyebrow to eyebrow, not separated by the least hair. What they share is the vajra mind-ground; what differs is only thought, emotion, love, and hate. Because the Buddhas and patriarchs make good use of their minds, they turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and transform a mountain of knives into a treasured grove, so that even the bitterest suffering and acrid pain all become the true realm of ultimate bliss. This is no other technique than that within this mind, thought and emotion are not born and love and hate find no lodging. It is like a clear eye that sees the open sky through and through — how then could there be inverted, illusory flowers arising and perishing of themselves? Sentient beings turn away from this, and no wonder they fall into all kinds of inversion and bring the fault upon themselves.]

He therefore taught him, saying: The Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings, birds and beasts, down to the three evil paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, as well as formless sentient beings — none of them are not joined eyebrow to eyebrow, without the least hair of difference. What they share is the vajra mind-ground; what differs is only thought, emotion, love, and hate. Because the Buddhas and patriarchs make good use of their vajra mind, they turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and transform a mountain of knives into a treasured grove; even the bitterest suffering and acrid pain all become the true realm of ultimate bliss. This is no other technique than that within this mind, thought and emotion are not born and love and hate find no lodging. It is like a clear eye that sees the open sky through and through — how then could it see inverted illusory flowers, arising and perishing of themselves? Sentient beings are entirely the opposite, taking thought, emotion, love, and hate as their mind; no wonder they fall into all kinds of confusion and inversion and falsely see illusory flowers arising and perishing — this is bringing the fault upon themselves.

[Emptied, scattered, dissolved, and sunk] This refers to formless sentient beings. The formless have no shape or color. Because of the delusion of inversion that scatters and dissolves them, such beings give rise to the karma of hidden, chaotic thought. Delusion and karma being dark and obscure, they are rewarded with this form of birth — that is, the class of the emptied, scattered, dissolved, and sunk. [Joined eyebrow to eyebrow] Joined as one body. The Gateless Gate says: “Chan Master Zhaozhou, asked by a monk, ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ answered, ‘No.’ Wumen (that is, the Chan monk Wumen Huikai, author of the book The Gateless Gate) said: In Chan practice one must pass through the patriarch’s gate, and in wondrous awakening one must exhaust the paths of mind. If the patriarch’s gate is not passed and the paths of mind are not cut off, one is nothing but a spirit clinging to grass and trees. But what is the patriarch’s gate? Just this one word No is a gate of the school. Hence he named it the gateless gate of Chan. One who passes through it not only sees Zhaozhou in person, but can walk hand in hand with the patriarchs of successive generations, joined eyebrow to eyebrow, seeing with the same eye and hearing with the same ear — is that not cause for rejoicing!” [The Gateless Gate] Wumen Huikai, a Chan monk of the Song dynasty, was asked for instruction by students, and so took the ancients’ public cases and made them into a tile for knocking at the gate, guiding students according to their capacities. He wrote them down as they came, and before he knew it they had become a collection. The book sets forth forty-eight famous public cases of old, together with verses and commentaries. [Vajra mind] That is, the original nature. Master Hanshan’s The Dream-Wandering Collection

Postface to the Vow of Bodhi Mind says: “All sages and ordinary beings alike are originally dwelling in the vajra mind-ground, complete with the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom.” In his commentary on the Diamond Sutra (Resolving the Doubts of the Diamond Sutra), Master Hanshan says: “The vajra mind is the fundamental mind with which the Buddha practiced the cause and realized the fruit. Now, coming into the world to teach sentient beings, he uses this mind entirely. He now teaches bodhisattvas to take the vajra mind as the root of their practice, as the first gate of entering the Mahāyāna.” “Now, to lead those formerly of the small vehicle to bring forth the Mahāyāna mind, he takes this vajra mind-ground as the root of practice.” [Illusory flowers] That is, flowers in empty space, a metaphor for illusions. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “What is ignorance? Good sons! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, fall into all kinds of inversion, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a person with a diseased eye who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky truly has no flowers; the sick person falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, he is not only confused about the nature of empty space but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From these false existences comes the turning round in birth and death; hence it is called ignorance.”

[The Buddhas and patriarchs, pitying such beings, came into the world expressly, and had no surplus dharma to give anyone: they did nothing but point directly at this mind, causing all sentient beings to know their home at once. Thus Vairocana, the Old One, when he first sat on the bodhi seat, likewise did no more than proclaim this precept-dharma of all the Buddhas of the past, the ten directions, and the three times. On the thousand-petal platform, Śākyamuni in every leaf and every world likewise did no more than declare this mind of all the Buddhas and proclaim this precept-dharma. Even the forty-nine years of wagging lips and flapping tongue, bustling here and there, bending and turning for people’s sake, did no more than cause all sentient beings universally to believe and accept this precept-dharma. And when at the very end he held up a flower, and gods and humans stared without understanding, they too were only deluded about this mind-precept. The golden-hued ascetic’s face broke into a smile, and so it passed through twenty-eight transmissions, hand to hand in succession; and when Bodhidharma came from the West and Shenguang stood in the snow, there were no words and no speech — all likewise a clear, direct pointing at this mind-precept.]

The Buddhas and patriarchs, pitying these inverted and deluded beings, came into the world expressly to teach, and had no other dharma to give anyone: they did nothing but point directly at this vajra mind, causing all sentient beings to know their home at once. Thus Vairocana Buddha, when he first sat on the bodhi seat, did no more than proclaim this vajra precious precept of all the Buddhas of the past, the ten directions, and the three times. On the thousand-petal platform, in each leaf a world, the Śākyamuni Buddha of each world likewise did no more than declare this mind of all the Buddhas and proclaim this precept-dharma. Even the forty-nine years of expounding sutras and preaching the Dharma, guiding with wholehearted care and explaining again and again for people’s sake, did no more than cause all sentient beings universally to believe and accept this precept-dharma. And when at the very end he held up a flower before the assembly, and gods and humans stared without understanding, they too were only deluded about this mind-precept (the vajra precious precepts). The golden-hued ascetic (Mahākāśyapa) broke into a smile, and so it passed through twenty-eight transmissions of Chan in the West, handed down in each generation; and when Bodhidharma (the first patriarch of Chan in China) came from the West and Shenguang (the second patriarch) stood in the snow and cut off his arm, there were no words and no speech — all were likewise a clear, direct pointing at this mind-precept.

[Holding up a flower] The Sutra of the Great Brahmā King Questioning the Buddha about Resolving Doubts says: The Brahmā King came to Vulture Peak and offered a golden utpala flower to Śākyamuni Buddha, requesting him to teach the Dharma. The World-Honored One held up the flower before the assembly and said nothing. At that moment a million humans and gods all failed to understand his meaning; only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the formless mark of reality, the subtle and wondrous Dharma gate, which is not established on words and is transmitted outside the teachings. I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. Śākyamuni Buddha first transmitted it to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: this is the beginning of the Chan school.

[Transmitted in turn through six generations, it reached Old Lu, the common fellow, who, beneath his load of firewood, heard the Diamond Sutra say, “Give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all,” and at once awakened to this precept — not obtained from others, not conferred by a teacher, but the nature itself complete. What is so extraordinary about that? When he came to Huangmei for confirmation, he at once said, “Originally there is not a single thing — where could dust cling?” Therefore the old man of Huangmei could do nothing with him either, and could only return to the abbot’s quarters without a word. Even the secret transmission at the third watch was very like swapping a man’s eyes for black beans — what was so extraordinary beyond this?]

Transmitted in turn through six generations in Chinese Chan, it reached Huineng, who beneath his load of firewood heard the Diamond Sutra say, “Give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all,” and thereupon at once awakened to this precept — not obtained from others, not conferred by a teacher, the self-nature being originally complete. What was so extraordinary beyond this? When he came to Huangmei (the Fifth Patriarch) for confirmation, he at once said, “Originally there is not a single thing — where could dust cling?” Therefore the Fifth Patriarch could do nothing with him either, and could only return to the abbot’s quarters without a word. Even the secret transmission of the robe and bowl at the third watch was very like swapping a man’s eyes for black beans — what was so extraordinary beyond this?
[Old Lu, the common fellow] That is, the Sixth Patriarch Huineng. Huineng’s secular surname was Lu, and at that time he had not yet left home, so he was called a common fellow.

[From this time on, sons and grandsons filled the eye and spread throughout the realm; those who obtained it died, those who lost it lived; the seventeen hundred (the seventeen hundred public cases), piping and playing, did no more than mutually illuminate one another in this mind-ground Dharma gate — how could it be that outside this mind one should seek a wondrous awakening elsewhere? If one seeks elsewhere apart from this, one falls into the crooked paths of outside teachings. Hence the Brahmā Net Sutra says: “The mind-ground of Vairocana Buddha, recited in the first arising of the mind, is named the Precept of Radiant Vajra Precious Precepts; it is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all bodhisattvas, the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings have Buddha-nature; all consciousness, form, and mind, whatever is feeling and whatever is mind, all enter the precept of Buddha-nature.” It also says: “When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they at once enter the rank of all Buddhas; their rank being equal to great awakening, they are truly the sons of the Buddhas.” Therefore in the fifty-five stages of progressive practice, one who has not seen Buddha-nature still falls upon the road
(the character is a variant of “road”)

of stages. Only when at the very end, in the stage of equal awakening, does it say: “This person first obtains the vajra mind, the initial stage of dry wisdom, and arriving here enters directly into the ocean of Buddha-nature.”]
